items.item: ZooKeeper guarantees linearizable writes and FIFO client order, implemented by the Zab atomic broadcast protocol; only writes are linearizable, so ordinary reads are served locally and can be stale.

at.step: Reveal: ZooKeeper's two guarantees, and a read that can lag behind them

items.item: An ephemeral znode is deleted automatically when the session that created it terminates, which is the building block leader-election recipes on ZooKeeper reuse, paired with a watch that notifies a client of the change.

items.item: etcd's KV API calls are strictly serializable by default; an opt-in serializable read may access stale data with respect to quorum but skips the live-consensus round trip.

items.item: Apache Kafka 4.0 is described in its own release announcement as the first major release to operate entirely without Apache ZooKeeper, replacing it with a Raft-replicated controller quorum that writes cluster metadata to a dedicated log.

at.step: Reveal: Kafka's own words — the first major release without ZooKeeper

items.item: Instead of majority vote, Kafka dynamically maintains a set of in-sync replicas and commits a write only once every member of that set has received it; to tolerate a given number of failures this needs one fewer replica than majority vote, at the cost of a commit waiting on the slowest in-sync member rather than the fastest.

at.step: Reveal: the in-sync set is a quorum, but not a majority one

items.item: With unclean leader election disabled, Kafka waits for a replica that was actually in the in-sync set to return as leader, favoring consistency; with it enabled, the first replica to return becomes leader even if it was never in sync, favoring availability over the acknowledged write.

at.step: Reveal: the trade a dropped setting makes, and the gap it still leaves

items.item: A last-replica-standing unclean shutdown can still turn a local data-loss event into a global one even with unclean leader election disabled, which KIP-966's Eligible Leader Replicas proposal addresses.

at.step: Reveal: the trade a dropped setting makes, and the gap it still leaves

items.item: An Iceberg table commit builds a new metadata file and replaces the old one with an atomic swap of a single catalog pointer, which is what gives table changes serializable isolation; a writer whose swap loses the race rebuilds against the new pointer and retries rather than failing outright.

at.step: Reveal: a table commit is one compare-and-swap on a single pointer

items.item: etcd is documented by Kubernetes as the consistent, highly-available key-value store used as its backing store for all cluster data, which is why etcd's own guarantees matter to anything built on Kubernetes' reconciliation loop.

at.deep: Internals: the hook's four combinations are two independent switches, not four special cases

items.item: Whether the hook's acknowledged write survives depends only on the unclean-leader-election setting once the leader and its in-sync follower both fail; min.insync.replicas changes how weak the starting acknowledgment was, not which setting decides survival after that specific failure.

at.step: Predict: which settings decide whether the acknowledged write survives?

items.item: Requiring read and write quorums each larger than half the replicas guarantees they intersect on at least one replica, but that intersection alone does not make a store linearizable; a protocol still needs a rule, such as versioning, for a read to pick out the overlapping replica's value over every other answer it receives.

at.step: Prove it: reads needing more than half the replicas and writes needing more than half — does that alone give a linearizable store?
